look_here_first: NATIVE WOODLAND BROME: follow an intact rooted plant to a PERSISTENT, non-rhizomatous perennial tuft, broad soft blades and an open drooping panicle. Under 10–20× inspect a 13–30 mm multi-flowered spikelet: lower glume normally ONE-veined (4–8 mm), upper THREE-veined (occasionally 5; 5–10 mm), and 8–12 mm lemmas usually hairy over the BACK (occasionally sparse or glabrous), each with a straight 3–8 mm awn. The 0.5–2 mm true membranous ligule has a jagged edge and no auricles. Introduced Japanese brome typically has more glume veins; native Texas brome also has a 1/3-veined pair but is ANNUAL. No existing target photo proves the glume veins, lemma hairs or ligule: keep FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.

best_field_traits: NATIVE WOODLAND BROME: look for a PERSISTENT PERENNIAL tuft in moist wooded ground with broad soft leaves, hairy sheaths and drooping branched panicles. The actual seed ID needs hairy lemma surfaces + roughly 3–8 mm awns and a mostly ONE-veined lower glume. Some introduced annual bromes also have hairy sheaths: this original low-res habit photo does NOT verify the lemma hairs.
GENUS: Bromus PANICLES carry MULTI-FLOWERED spikelets; outer pair = GLUMES, inner overlapping units = LEMMAS, often with AWNS; not a true Hordeum/Elymus rachis SPIKE.
Native perennial of shaded or moist woodland understory; intact old crown is essential to confirm perennial habit.
Relatively broad grass blades, frequently soft hairy closed sheaths, long arching leafy flowering culms.
Open drooping panicle, many-flowered spikelets frequently ~13–30 mm; the original low-res photo supports habit only.
Fertile lemma short straight awn often ~3–8 mm, not strongly long/curved like mature Japanese brome.
Rescuegrass B. catharticus is COMPARISON ONLY: large BROAD FLATTENED spikelets with short or no awns; many awned bromes differ from it.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: High-res whole plant with base showing perennial crown
Visible lower closed sheath and hairy node closeup
Glumes, lemmas, and whether mature upper internodes are hairy
crew_field_check: LOOK AT THE SPIKELET, NOT JUST THE DROOP: all four bromes have several florets stacked along one spikelet, often with lemma awns. First decide ANNUAL vs PERENNIAL, then count florets, measure the entire spikelet, individual lemma and awn, and inspect the glume veins and leaf sheath hairs. Nodding inflorescences or long awns alone are not a species ID.
Measure actual mature spikelet(s) with a millimeter ruler.
Inspect lemma/glume or true ligule ONLY where detailed pixels or a collected macro are actually available.
Record uncertain grass to genus, don't force the species from one photo.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Japanese brome — Bromus japonicus: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair. Lanceolate brome — Bromus lanceolatus: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle. Hairy woodland brome — Bromus pubescens: Native North American woodland perennial, often taller with broader soft leaves, and open drooping panicle. Shorter generally straight lemma awns commonly 3–8 mm. Lower glume typically 1-veined; true pubescence may be obvious on entire lemma. Texas brome — Bromus texensis: Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm. Rescuegrass — Bromus catharticus (comparison only): Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).

field_matrix.where_to_look: At flowering inspect loose kinked/arching panicle BRANCHES; at fruit inspect lower/upper glume VEINS on intact source-verified spikelet.
field_matrix.look_alike: Introduced cool-season annual. Usually small-to-moderate narrow awned spikelets on flexible, often nodding/kinked panicle branches. Flora of North America typically gives lower glume 3–5 veins, upper 7 veins; separate from native Texas brome's 1/3-veined pair.
field_matrix.confirmation: Open macro: overlapping lemmas have long often twisted/recurving awns from below their apices; source descriptions vary considerably in spikelet length. Do not use a 10–15 mm cutoff to exclude Japanese brome.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: Nodding and awns also occur in native Texas brome; compare intact mature glumes and source-labelled specimen.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Use whole flowering panicle + intact mature multi-flowered spikelet measurements together.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Measure an intact mature spikelet including ALL florets excluding its awns, then count fertile florets.
field_matrix.look_alike: Introduced annual. Typically larger long lance-shaped spikelets ~25–50 mm, with roughly 8–20 florets and ~12–18 mm mature lemmas; open panicle.
field_matrix.confirmation: Compare long often pointed spikelets with Japanese brome's often smaller fewer florets, but both dimensions vary; check true lemma body and awn attachment at 10–20×.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: Length alone overlaps rescuegrass and native bromes; always count florets and inspect glumes.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Use whole flowering panicle + intact mature multi-flowered spikelet measurements together.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Measure mature spikelet, glumes and lemma at mm scale; count veins on BOTH persistent GLUMES.
field_matrix.look_alike: Texas-native annual restricted to limited Texas sites. Flora of North America: often 20–30 mm spikelets with 4–7 florets, lower glume ONE vein (~6–9 mm), upper THREE (~8–10.5 mm), lemma ~9–15 mm and awn ~4–8 mm.
field_matrix.confirmation: This 1/3 vein pair distinguishes from Japanese's commonly higher 3–5/7 vein counts. The lemma apex described as entire by FNA but sometimes toothed in other treatments: DO NOT force an ID from 'two teeth'.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: This is a botanically important native versus introduced split. Preserve TAXON/RANGE decisions and label uncertain lookalikes Bromus sp.; Hays County origin NOT proven from these photo references.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Inspect a mature INTACT glume pair and count actual longitudinal veins, not awns or background photos.

field_matrix.where_to_look: Whole flowering panicle: look for big FLAT, broad, oat-like spikelets with very SHORT or absent awns.
field_matrix.look_alike: Introduced South American cool-season grass, often annual or short-lived perennial depending ecology/treatment. Larger broad 16–40 mm strongly flattened spikelets, many florets and short/no awns (often 0–4 mm).
field_matrix.confirmation: Large flattened overlapping V/oat-like florets contrast with Japanese brome's narrow long-awned units and lanceolate brome's narrower long densely floret spikelets.
field_matrix.avoid_false_identification: Not installed in learner. Annual-versus-perennial is NOT sufficient: Texas A&M treats annual, Kew often perennial.
field_matrix.quick_rule: Use whole flowering panicle + intact mature multi-flowered spikelet measurements together.

not_reliable_alone: One awn length, purple seedhead color, or an overall nodding silhouette without attached spikelets.
Soft hair on lower SHEATH: found on multiple introduced and native Bromus species.
Whole head length alone: Flora of North America, Kew GrassBase and Texas regional treatments report overlapping but non-identical ranges.
Lower and upper glume vein count from a photograph that doesn't actually resolve the glumes under backlight.
Presence of yellow extruded ANTHERS: diagnostic of flowering grass stage, NOT Bromus texensis species.
An apparently perennial tuft when broken roots or mowing obscure annual/reproductive life cycle.
Unreviewed county nativity; rare native Texas brome may resemble introduced Japanese brome.

field_id_finish_pass.crew_teaching_summary: Native North American woodland PERENNIAL with a fairly tall loose, drooping flowering head, relatively broad soft leaves, and hairy sheaths. Check a true membranous ligule and awned multi-flowered spikelets. This existing photograph is low resolution, so lemma-level confirmation remains OPEN.
field_id_finish_pass.lookalike_comparison: Unlike the three other currently installed Bromus cards, B. pubescens is PERENNIAL and often found in shaded moist woodland understory. Japanese brome is a small-spikeleted annual with flexuous panicle branches; B. lanceolatus has unusually long, many-flowered annual spikelets; B. texensis is an annual with shorter awns and requires mature glume/lemma comparison. Habitat or hairiness alone cannot clinch this one.

measured_reproductive_field_key_20261024.look_here_first: Confirm rooted perennial bunch + open often nodding panicle, then a mature attached spikelet and its two glumes. Hairy sheath or drooping seedhead alone does not identify species.
measured_reproductive_field_key_20261024.measurable_habit_and_collar: Perennial, non-rhizomatous; culms typically 65–120(150) cm, open often nodding panicles 10–25 cm. Leaf blades generally 6–19 mm wide. Closed sheaths commonly have backward-pointing (retrorse) hairs. True membranous ligule 0.5–2 mm, truncate/erose edge, no auricles; inspect blade–sheath junction with 1-mm ruler.
measured_reproductive_field_key_20261024.measurable_spikelet_glumes: Spikelets (13)15–30 mm long, commonly 5–10 (overall 4–13) florets. At spikelet BASE identify TWO persistent glumes: LOWER 4–8 mm, typically 1 vein; UPPER 5–10 mm, usually 3 veins, sometimes 5. Glumes are generally awnless and often hairy, but pubescence varies.
measured_reproductive_field_key_20261024.measurable_lemma_palea_awn: Each fertile lemma typically 8–12 mm, about 5–7 veined depending treatment; back and margins commonly finely hairy, sometimes nearly glabrous. One straight awn usually 3–8 mm arises near/below lemma apex (within ~1.5 mm in Flora of North America-derived description). Palea is slightly shorter and often ciliate along its keels. Do not mistake glume tips for lemma awns. Lemma-tip terminology differs among sources (entire/acute versus minutely notched); do not force an ID from apparent teeth.
local_lookalike_split: B. japonicus (introduced annual): lower glume generally 3–5-veined and upper often 7-veined, unlike pubescens 1 and usually 3. Drooping/kinked panicle alone is insufficient.

B. texensis (native annual): ALSO usually 1-veined lower and 3-veined upper glume, so vein counts alone do not separate it. Confirm rooted ANNUAL versus PERENNIAL crown, mature lemma pubescence and other reproductive dimensions; preserve unreviewed county status.
B. lanceolatus (introduced annual): much longer narrow 25–50 mm spikelets, commonly 8–20 florets; compare intact spikelets and rooted base.
B. catharticus (introduced rescuegrass; comparison only): broad flattened spikelets with short or absent awns; inspect a complete head and mature floret.
crew_steps: 1. Photograph a WHOLE rooted specimen, show old perennial crown and full open 10–25 cm flowering panicle; do not infer longevity from a cropped stem.
2. At the blade–sheath junction open the CLOSED sheath; document 0.5–2 mm erose membranous ligule, absent auricles and direction of sheath hairs.
3. Isolate three mature attached spikelets with 1-mm scale; count florets and measure body without awns.
4. Separate and backlight BOTH basal glumes; count 1 versus usually 3 veins, and record glume lengths before handling the lemmas.
5. Turn a fertile 8–12 mm lemma DORSAL face toward lens; document fine hairs over the back and margins (allow rare sparse/glabrous specimens), 5–7 veins, straight 3–8 mm awn and insertion.
6. Compare mature B. japonicus and B. texensis at matched scale; if glume veins/crown cannot be observed, leave Bromus sp. provisional.
NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: Exact-source, locally verified connected rooted B. pubescens perennial crown plus intact panicle; centimeter scale and Hays-area voucher/context.
Actual blade–sheath junction split open in face/profile, 1-mm scale resolving erose 0.5–2 mm TRUE membrane, absent auricles and retrorse hairs.
Three mature 13–30 mm multi-flowered spikelets with 1-mm scale and individually exposed LOWER 1-veined 4–8 mm / UPPER 3(5)-veined 5–10 mm glumes.
Dissected 8–12 mm lemma dorsal face under 10–20× showing real back/margin hairs (or explicitly documented hairless variant), awn origin and palea; calibrated ruler.
Same-angle, matched-scale B. japonicus and B. texensis glume pairs and basal crowns; public-licensed, exact-species source evidence.
NEEDS_SITE_QA: Verify existing two local species JPEGs and source/creator/public-rights metadata; do not relabel EPA public domain or Daderot CC0.
Inspect two existing gross-feature arrows on original EPA image at actual rendered resolution; do not add fine anatomy arrows to unresolvable pixels.
Verify any newly acquired photos have exact taxon identity, individual image license, attribution, sanitized bytes and calibrated arrow coordinates before public-ready status.
Check ordinary Visual Learner mobile display and source/rights badges after a separate authorized site lane; no Pages deployment claimed by this commit.

Do not mark FINISHED from text-only measurements or the two current habit images.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Hairy woodland brome — first see the real spikelet, then measure
steps: START with both archived exact-species photographs; trace the branching panicle to a single multi-flowered spikelet, then locate the rooted basal crown where actually visible. Never conclude a rhizomatous perennial merely from one photographic frame.

CHECK woody-shaded habitat and a persistent perennial base as supporting characters. Japanese, lanceolate and Texas bromes are annuals in the existing comparison key; habitat or duration alone cannot settle an uncertain taxon.
MATURE SPIKELET WITH SCALE: expect 5–10(13) florets and a roughly 15–30 mm spikelet (outer extremes around 13 mm); isolate lower and upper glumes rather than counting overlapping lemmas as glumes.

GLUME/LEMMA MACRO: lower glume typically 1-veined, upper 3(5)-veined; lemmas about 8–12 mm, often hairy on backs and margins but sometimes glabrous/scabrous. Never use lemma hairiness alone to exclude this species; photograph several ripe florets and count under backlight.

AWN AND LIGULE: mature lemma awns typically 4–7(8) mm, arising within 1.5 mm below apex; true membranous ligule 0.5–2 mm. Photograph with 1-mm ruler; sheath retrorse hairs and node hairs are separate structures.

COMPARE authentic B. pubescens against locally relevant B. texensis and introduced B. japonicus with matched mature spikelets. Record lower/upper glume venation and fertile lemma lengths, not just panicle droop.
If the photographed hair insertion or perennial crown is not demonstrable, retain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS and record Bromus sp. where field material is unresolved.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: WOODED PERENNIAL BROME: confirm durable crown and true hairs on mature lemmas; match a measured spikelet and sheath/collar photo before separating native pubescens from annual bromes.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Both local gallery images verified in metadata, but neither proves a measured lemma, ligule or glume anatomy. Hairiness is variable and glumes may themselves be pubescent; do not teach glumes as invariably glabrous. Measurements are literature ranges, not verified from the two site images. No new photograph or arrow added.
field_photo_quickcheck.featured_index_note: featured_photo_indices [0,1] refer to the TWO images[] species records; actual seven-panel visual_comparison target-species indices are [0,6]. Panels 1–5 are different Bromus look-alikes.

what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Same source-authenticated B. pubescens perennial with connected rooted non-rhizomatous crown, full 10–25 cm flowering panicle, habitat and centimeter ruler; do not use a cropped garden tuft as root proof.
Open the actual inner blade–sheath junction on that plant and measure its 0.5–2 mm erose membranous ligule with a 1-mm scale; separately photograph closed sheath and direction of retrorse hairs.
Photograph two or three ripe attached spikelets beside a millimeter scale: record total (13)15–30 mm spikelet body and typically 5–10 florets, excluding awns from body length.

Separate and backlight the TWO basal glumes of the same ripe spikelet: lower 4–8 mm usually one-veined, upper 5–10 mm usually three-veined (occasionally five); never infer vein counts from habit panels.
Photograph the dorsal face of a removed 8–12 mm mature fertile lemma and shorter palea, showing actual variable back/margin hairs, palea keels and measured near-apical straight 3–8 mm awn insertion.

Obtain matched species-confirmed native B. texensis and introduced B. japonicus glume/lemma photos at the same scale; both B. pubescens and B. texensis can share the 1/3 glume pattern, so crown and lemma matter.

NEEDS_SITE_QA: verify EPA public-domain and Daderot CC0 source/creator/bytes, all seven correctly labelled panels (B. pubescens only 0 and 6), existing gross arrows, rights-filtered mobile rendering and EXIF/GPS rules; add no microscopic arrow without visible anatomy.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — WOODLAND PERENNIAL BROME
field_id_short_tiles.short: Follow a loose, often drooping panicle to a persistent, non-rhizomatous perennial bunch; confirm on mature spikelets, not droop alone.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Hairy woodland brome is a native perennial of mesic wooded sites, with culms commonly 65–120(150) cm, relatively soft blades 6–19 mm wide, and open 10–25 cm panicles. A rooted persistent crown is important because native Texas brome and introduced Japanese/lanceolate bromes are annuals. EPA and Copenhagen photos plus new true in-ground Austin woodland-habit panel 8 show different stages and live leafy bunching, but NOT an extracted connected perennial crown or perennial age proof.
field_id_short_tiles.status: THREE SAME-SPECIES HABIT VIEWS (TEXAS WOODLAND INCLUDED) — EXPOSED PERENNIAL ROOTS STILL MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE TRUE COLLAR — MEMBRANOUS LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Look inside the blade–sheath junction for a 0.5–2 mm erose membrane; no auricles.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Open a fresh leaf at the inner collar and measure the short 0.5–2 mm glabrous membranous ligule with a 1-mm ruler. It is not the often retrorse hairs on the CLOSED sheath or hairy nodes. Leaf blades are usually 6–19 mm wide; sheaths may be conspicuously hairy but can vary. Do not use sheath pubescence alone to determine species. Actual newly archived panels 7 (blade/sheath exterior) and 9 (true culm joint) show the correct STRUCTURES to examine, but neither opens the short INNER ligule at a calibrated 1-mm scale. It remains a photographic hold, not an arrow target.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REAL EXTERIOR SHEATH AND NODE PHOTOGRAPHED — TRUE INNER LIGULE/MM SCALE NOT CERTIFIED

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE A RIPE MULTIFLORED SPIKELET
field_id_short_tiles.short: Usually 15–30 mm (occasionally ~13 mm) with about 5–10 florets; outer pair are glumes.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Choose 2–3 ripe, source-authenticated spikelets still attached to the branched panicle, measure their complete length and count florets under 10–20×. Published ranges include (13)15–30 mm and (4)5–10(13) florets. The two basal persistent bracts are GLUMES; the overlapping bracts around individual florets are LEMMAS. New exact-species source photos 10 and 11 show fresh and dry real Texas spikelets. The comparison photos in panels 1–5 show DIFFERENT Bromus species; never use them as proof of pubescens reproductive dimensions or assert these fresh photos have measured floret counts.
field_id_short_tiles.status: FRESH AND DRY REAL TEXAS MULTIFLORED SPIKELETS PHOTOGRAPHED; ACTUAL SCALE/FLORET COUNTS PENDING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · GLUME VEINS — IMPORTANT NATIVE/INTRODUCED SPLIT
field_id_short_tiles.short: Lower glume 4–8 mm, usually ONE vein; upper 5–10 mm, usually THREE (rarely five).
field_id_short_tiles.details: Dissect the basal glume pair from a ripe B. pubescens spikelet. Under transmitted light count the lower glume's usual 1 vein and upper glume's usual 3 (sometimes 5) veins; both are normally awnless. Japanese brome often has substantially more glume veins, but native Texas brome ALSO has the 1/3 pattern. Therefore 1/3 glumes do NOT by themselves prove woodland brome: compare rooted life history and mature lemmas. The additional exact-species fresh and dry green/bract views (panels 10/11) are not backlit or separated into individual glumes; no exact-species photo supports a vein-count arrow.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · HAIRY LEMMA, PALEA AND STRAIGHT AWN
field_id_short_tiles.short: Mature lemma 8–12 mm, often hairy across back and margins; straight awn usually 3–8 mm.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Remove one mature floret and distinguish the 8–12 mm LEMMA from the usually shorter PALEA, whose keels may be ciliate. The lemma commonly has fine hairs on the back and margins but can be sparse or nearly glabrous; never reject pubescens solely because one floret looks smooth. Measure its single straight ~3–8 mm awn emerging near/below the apex (usually within ~1.5 mm). Descriptions of tiny lemma-tip teeth differ; do not fabricate a bifid apex. A new dry actual species spikelet macro in panel 11 better shows real overlapping elongated bracts and awns, but it still cannot certify separate dorsal hair insertion, palea keels or awn origin from these pixels.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES AND PUBLIC-READY GATE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Texas brome shares 1/3-veined glumes but is annual; Japanese brome has more glume veins; rescuegrass has broad flat spikelets.
field_id_short_tiles.details: B. texensis (panel 2) is a native annual with often 1/3-veined glumes, so protect it from misidentification; B. japonicus (panel 1) is an introduced annual, commonly with higher glume vein counts; B. lanceolatus (panel 3) is introduced with long ~25–50 mm many-flowered spikelets; B. catharticus (panels 4–5) is comparison-only and has broader flattened, short/no-awn spikelets. These are look-alike photos, not pubescens anatomy evidence. NEW five Texas source-labelled real woodland photos at panels 7–11 now show an actual in-ground bunch, external sheath and stem node, living green and dry spikelets; none exposes an intact 0.5–2-mm true ligule, connected extracted perennial root system, backlit glumes or separated hairy lemma. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: same-plant rooted crown/panicle, true measured ligule, backlit glume pair and hairy mature lemma with scale. NEEDS_SITE_QA: exact rights, provenance, annotations, comparison labels and mobile gallery. Retain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS until evidence and live QA are verified.
